pages.title: Aristotle as father of comparative politics
pages.summary: Poses the question on comparative government, its evolution and the limits of the traditional method. Notes say Aristotle applied the biological method of classification to 158 constitutions, grouping them by number and purpose, and that the discipline evolved in two phases, up to and after the Second World War.

pages.title: Features of traditional versus modern comparative politics
pages.summary: Traditional comparative politics studied western constitutions through the legal-institutional approach because the non-western world was colonised. After the Second World War new states emerged and focus shifted to developing areas under the influence of Behaviouralism.

pages.title: Limitations of traditional comparative politics
pages.summary: Lists the limitations: parochial, ethnocentric (Eurocentric belief that non-Europeans were barbaric and imperialism a civilising mission), static and textual, a study of government rather than politics, and essentially non-comparative because the western world is one world.

pages.title: Descriptive methods and rise of modern comparative politics
pages.summary: Traditional methods were descriptive and less analytical. In new non-western states constitutions existed without constitutionalism, so extra-constitutional factors had to be studied, giving rise to the systems approach, structural functional approach, political culture, political sociology and political economy.

pages.title: Systems Approach: David Easton and the system concept
pages.summary: Systems Approach is a behavioural approach given by David Easton, influenced by General Systems Theory from biology and first used in sociology by Talcott Parsons. A system is a set of elements in patterned interaction, like the circulatory system.

pages.title: Political system, boundary, environment, authoritative allocation
pages.summary: The diagram shows the political system interacting with social, economic, cultural and international systems inside a boundary. The political system is separated from others by its unique function, the authoritative allocation of values through legally binding decisions.

pages.title: Easton's input-output model: demands and supports
pages.summary: Easton likens the political system to a machine in which demands and support enter as inputs and are converted into decisions and policies, with a feedback loop. The notes list four types of demand and four types of support.

pages.title: Easton's outputs and criticism of Systems Approach
pages.summary: Four outputs are extraction, regulation of behaviour, allocation of goods and services, and symbolic output. Traditionalists call the model cosmetic, jargon-heavy and only a conceptual framework, while Marxists call it biased towards western liberal democracy, not value free and status quoist.

pages.title: Systems Approach: protest gap and conclusion
pages.summary: The model has no scope to explain social protest, social movements and revolution. The conclusion credits it for the urge to make politics scientific and for showing the need to look beyond constitutions to environmental factors.

pages.title: Structural Functional Approach: Almond, Powell and influences
pages.summary: Almond and Powell built it to study developing areas and to cure Easton's model, which is too general and lacks detail on structures and functions. Influences named are Easton, Lucian Pye's political development, Malinowski's functionalism and the legal-institutional approach.

pages.title: Four input and three output functions with structures
pages.summary: The diagram pairs input functions (socialisation and recruitment, communication, interest articulation, interest aggregation) and output functions (rule making, application, adjudication) with their structures. Its advantages over the systems approach are detail and better comparison, since political systems are at different stages of development.

pages.title: Criticism and contribution of structural functionalism
pages.summary: Traditionalist and Marxist criticisms repeat those of the systems approach: western bias and status quoism with no scope to explain crisis or protest. Its contributions are a framework for organising data, a detailed view of structures and functions, and a more dynamic outlook than the systems approach.

flashcards.front: Why is Aristotle regarded as the Father of comparative politics?
flashcards.back: Aristotle applied the method of classification found in Biology to the study of constitutions. He studied 158 constitutions and classified them on the basis of number and purpose, one of the earliest uses of the comparative method.

flashcards.front: List the main limitations of traditional comparative politics.
flashcards.back: It was parochial (narrow to western countries), ethnocentric, static and textual, a study of comparative government rather than politics, essentially non-comparative because the western world is one world, and more descriptive than analytical.

flashcards.front: Why did modern comparative politics need methods beyond the study of constitutions?
flashcards.back: In non-western countries there is a big gap between theory and practice: constitutions exist but constitutionalism does not. So extra-constitutional factors such as society, culture, economic development and modernisation had to be studied.

flashcards.front: What is the unique function that, in Easton's Systems Approach, separates the political system from other systems?
flashcards.back: The authoritative allocation of values. The political system is the main decision-making body with authority, so its decisions are legally binding.

flashcards.front: How do Marxists criticise Easton's Systems Approach?
flashcards.back: They say it is biased towards the western liberal democratic system, so it is not value free despite claiming to be scientific. It presents western systems as the ideal type and is status quoist, since the feedback loop suggests the system responds smoothly to people's aspirations.

flashcards.front: Why did Almond and Powell develop the Structural Functional Approach?
flashcards.back: To build a model usable for the study of developing areas and to address defects in Easton's model, which is too general and gives no detailed view of the structures and functions within a political system.

flashcards.front: Which structures correspond to the input and output functions in the Structural Functional Approach?
flashcards.back: Socialisation and recruitment: family, kinship groups, educational institutions; communication: mass media; interest articulation: pressure groups; interest aggregation: political parties. Rule making: legislature; rule application: executive; rule adjudication: judiciary.

flashcards.front: How is the Structural Functional Approach more dynamic than the Systems Approach?
flashcards.back: It accepts that different political systems are at different stages of development. For example, developed societies have more associational pressure groups and technology-based communication, while developing societies have more community-based groups and caste-based parties.

answers.question: Discuss the salient features of the Systems Approach. Do you think the Systems Approach is status quoist?
answers.intro: The Systems Approach, a behavioural and scientific approach given by David Easton, treats politics as a system of patterned interaction with its environment. It was drawn from General Systems Theory in Biology and Talcott Parsons's use of systems in sociology.
body: A system is a set of elements in patterned interaction, with a boundary and an environment made up of social, economic, cultural and international systems. The political system is distinguished by its unique function, the authoritative allocation of values, meaning its decisions are legally binding.

Easton compares the political system to a machine working on an input-output mechanism. Demands (for goods and services, regulation of behaviour, participation, communication) and supports (material support, obedience to law, participation, attention to government communication) are converted into decisions and policies, with a feedback loop.
Outputs are of four types: extraction such as taxes, regulation of behaviour, allocation of goods and services, and symbolic outputs such as respect for the flag and anthem.

Traditionalists call it cosmetic, jargon-heavy and only a conceptual framework. Marxists call it status quoist and biased towards western liberal democracy, since the feedback loop shows smooth responsiveness and leaves no scope to explain protest, social movements or revolution.
answers.conclusion: Despite its status quoist bias and western orientation, the approach reflects the urge to make the study of politics scientific. It showed that politics cannot be understood through constitutions alone and that environmental factors must be studied.

answers.question: Why did traditional comparative politics prove inadequate after the Second World War? Examine how modern approaches responded to its limitations.
answers.intro: Comparative politics began with Aristotle's classification of 158 constitutions and, until the Second World War, studied mainly western countries through the legal-institutional approach. The emergence of new states exposed the limits of that method.
body: Traditional comparative politics was parochial and ethnocentric. It concentrated on western countries and, being Eurocentric, assumed that people outside Europe were barbaric and that imperialism was a civilising mission.

It was static and textual because it studied constitutions and institutions while neglecting social and cultural factors and political processes. It was comparative government rather than comparative politics, and essentially non-comparative since the western world is one world with little contrast. Its methods were descriptive, not analytical.

After the Second World War many non-western countries gained independence. In them constitutions exist but constitutionalism does not, so a big gap between theory and practice appeared. Extra-constitutional factors such as society, culture, economic development and modernisation became essential.

Modern methods followed under the influence of Behaviouralism, with maximum use of behavioural method in this discipline: the systems approach of Easton, the structural functional approach of Almond and Powell, political culture, political sociology and political economy, with focus shifting to developing areas.
answers.conclusion: Traditional comparative politics gave the discipline its starting point but could not explain politics outside the West. Modern methods made it analytical and global, and today comparative politics is a vibrant discipline with extensive ongoing research.
